beats.intro: Lesson nineteen. [[sub]]Three invisible forces steer what people do at work: the market, the contract, and culture.
beats.drive: Grove starts with a drive. [[tires]]You need new tires. You compare dealers, maybe check a consumer magazine, and buy what meets your needs at the lowest cost. You are thinking only of yourself. You would never tell the dealer he is charging too little. [[light]]Then you reach a red light, and you stop, without a thought. Society has set a rule that everyone stops, and a traffic cop penalizes anyone who doesn't. [[crash]]Further on, you come upon a serious accident. Now you forget the rules and your own interest. You help the victims, even at some risk to yourself. [[care]]What moves you now is concern for someone else's life.
beats.three: Three moments, three different forces. [[work]]Grove says our behaviour at work is steered by the same three, invisible and everywhere. [[m1]]Free-market forces. [[m2]]Contractual obligations. [[m3]]And cultural values. [[road]]Each one matches a stop on that drive.
beats.market: Start with the market. [[two]]Two parties trade goods or services. They might be people, groups or whole companies, and each is out only for itself. [[price]]I want to buy at the lowest price. You want to sell at the highest. [[broke]]Neither cares if the other goes broke, and neither pretends to. [[eff]]It is very efficient. No one needs to oversee it, because everyone openly serves their own interest. [[but]]So why not use it everywhere? Because it only works when the thing traded has a clear dollar value. Tires do. Much of what passes between people at work does not.
beats.contract: Between companies, the market usually rules: you buy a commodity part at the best price you can get. [[team]]But when a group of people does the work together, what is each engineer's share worth? [[bit]]If you bought engineering by the bit, you would spend more time pricing each bit than the bit is worth. [[deal]]So you make a deal instead. I hire you for a year, for a set amount, to do a certain kind of work. I give you an office and a terminal, and you promise to do your best. [[auth]]I can't spell out every day in advance, so the contract gives me general authority: to monitor your work, evaluate it, and correct it if needed. [[rules]]And we agree on rules we will both obey.
beats.overhead: Think of the red light again. [[green]]We stop on red because we count on others doing the same, so we can drive through on green. [[cop]]But for people who break the rule, we need police. And with police, as with supervisors, comes overhead. [[tax]]Taxes are a contract too. We give up part of what we earn and expect services back, and it takes a giant apparatus to audit the returns. [[util]]Or take a utility. It offers to build a three-hundred-million-dollar power plant, if no one else may sell electricity in that region. The state agrees, [[puc]]but sets up a Public Utilities Commission to decide what the utility may charge, and how much profit it may make. [[mono]]A monopoly, in exchange for accepting the rules.
beats.culture: Now the third mode. [[when]]Sometimes the world changes faster than anyone can rewrite the rules. Or a situation is so unclear that a contract covering every case would be hopelessly complicated. [[group]]Then control comes from cultural values. Its mark: the interest of the group comes before the interest of the individual. [[trust]]That brings in loaded words like trust, because you hand the group your ability to protect yourself. [[share]]You will only do that if you believe you all share the same values, the same objectives and the same methods. [[exp]]And those grow only from a great deal of shared experience.
beats.mgmt: So what does management do in each mode? [[flea]]In a market, nothing. No one supervises the sales at a flea market. [[cmgr]]Under a contract, managers set and change the rules, monitor whether they are kept, and evaluate and improve performance. [[cult]]Under cultural values, managers must build and nurture the shared values, objectives and methods that trust depends on. [[say]]One way is to spell them out. [[ex]]The other, and more important, way is by example. [[match]]When people see your behaviour match the values you profess, a group culture grows.
beats.q3: Quick check. Which mode is the manager working in?
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]In a market, each side serves itself, and price decides. [[w2]]A contract trades pay for rules and general authority, and monitoring it costs overhead. [[w3]]Contracts fit where value is too hard to price. [[w4]]Culture puts the group first, and rests on trust built from shared experience. [[w5]]Managers build culture by spelling out values, and even more by living them. Now the lesson practice.

beats.finish: Well done. That is the end of lesson nineteen. Next: how to choose the right mode.
